# Abstract

This gazetteer catalogues 192 early modern urban settlements, fortress citadels, riverine market towns and nomadic seasonal commercial centres active across Central Asia between 1500AD and 1865AD (encompassing 3.890.946 km² across eight territorial units). Synthesising regional Islamic judicial archives, waqf endowment cadastres, water allocation records and early Russian imperial demographic surveys [@Anon2016Visions; @Gafurova2026Waqf; @Nurullayeva2025Timurid; @Anarbaeva2025Socio; @Wang2026Russian; @Razdykov2019Appearance], the compendium encompasses every primary documented habitation centre of the domain. These entries span the massive commercial and industrial metropolis of Tashkent (peaking at 133,9k inhabitants in 1850AD), the venerable theological and political capitals of Bukhara (90k) and Samarkand (85k), the rapidly expanding hydraulic cities of the Ferghana Valley led by Kokand (78k), Namangan (53,3k), Andijan (42k) and Margilan (34k), the deltaic fortress capital of Khiva (30k), and vital steppe commercial hubs including Turkistan (28k), Saraishyk (24k), Semey (22,6k) and Oral (31,4k) [@Nurullayeva2025Timurid; @Anarbaeva2025Socio; @Croix2021Roundtable]. Across the 192 catalogued entries, the gazetteer records longitudinal demographic developments spanning the initial Shaybanid consolidation, seventeenth-century trade expansion, the mid-eighteenth-century Dzungar and Afsharid crises and the nineteenth-century agricultural resurgence. Alongside the 192 catalogued settlements, the regional source ledger records 17 excluded duplicate historical aliases and peripheral boundary entries out of 209 total evaluated candidate entities.

# Background

Early modern settlement systems in Central Asia reflected an intricate functional specialisation between sedentary oasis urbanism and nomadic pastoral logistical nodes [@Nurullayeva2025Timurid; @StephanEmmrich2018Mobilities]. In Transoxiana, oasis cities developed behind massive sun-dried mudbrick fortifications (*devol*) reinforced by semicircular towers and deep moats [@Nurullayeva2025Timurid]. Within these defensive perimeters lay an elevated citadel (*ark*) housing the ruler's palace, treasury and garrison, surrounded by a densely built commercial and residential city (*shahristan*) [@Nurullayeva2025Timurid; @Anon2016Visions]. Public spaces were organised around domed market intersections (*taqi* or *chorsu*), bathhouses, public cisterns (*sardoba*) and monumental Friday mosques paired with theological colleges (*madrasa*) [@Nurullayeva2025Timurid; @Gafurova2026Waqf]. Outside the main gates lay expansive suburban quarters (*rabat*), potteries, brick kilns, flour mills and irrigated orchards [@Anon2016Visions; @Mamurov2024Nationwide].

Across the Ferghana Valley, the hydraulic statecraft of the Ming Khanate transformed Kokand, Namangan, Andijan and Margilan into specialised manufacturing and agricultural hubs, where craft guilds produced silk brocades, glazed ceramics and Damascus steel blades [@Anarbaeva2025Socio; @Jabbarov2023Patterns]. In Khwarazm, Khiva served as a protected fortress oasis whose brick walls (Ichan Kala and Dishan Kala) shielded royal complexes, minarets and madrasas from desert dust storms and nomadic raids [@Croix2021Roundtable].

North of the agrarian frontier, settlement took the form of fortified riverine entreposts and strategic seasonal camps [@Razdykov2019Appearance; @Wang2026Russian]. Towns such as Turkistan (anchored by the monumental Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi), Sayram and Sauran served as essential exchange points where Kazakh pastoralists traded livestock for textiles, tea and metal implements [@Karassayev2025History; @Rasulov2021Importance]. In western Kazakhstan, Saraishyk on the Ural River functioned as an administrative and trade centre for the Junior Zhuz before its destruction by Cossacks, while Oral (Uralsk) and Semey (Semipalatinsk) grew into Russian frontier fortress towns coordinating regional steppe commerce [@Wang2026Russian; @Toraigyrov2026Topical].

# Methodology

Settlement records were compiled by extracting documented historical settlements from municipal registers, waqf cadastres, archaeological excavation inventories (notably the UCL Central Asian Archaeological Landscapes database) and nineteenth-century military topography surveys [@Anon2016Visions; @Gafurova2026Waqf; @Nurullayeva2025Timurid; @Wang2026Russian]. All 192 catalogued settlements possess verified geocoded WGS84 coordinates and assign to one of the eight territorial units.

In the regional source ledger, 17 candidate records were excluded as duplicate historical aliases (such as variant transliterations of Kokand, Bukhara, Andijan and Margilan) or peripheral entries situated beyond canonical domain boundaries (such as Andakhudh and Babna in northern Afghanistan) [@Anon2016Visions; @Bleuer2012State]. All municipal administrative entities and surrounding suburban village clusters were consolidated into unified urban entries with longitudinal demographic series.

# Testing and Validation

Source ledger reconciliation confirms 192 included settlements and 17 excluded candidate entries, accounting for all 209 evaluated entities without discrepancy. All 192 settlements possess verified geographic coordinates and chronologically bounded population estimates. Figure \ref{fig:sett-gazetteer} displays the rank-size distribution and the leading early modern urban centres across Central Asia through 1865AD.

## Sub-Regional Distribution and Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:regsum-early-modern} summarises the distribution of catalogued settlements across all eight territories alongside their leading centres. The Khanate of Kokand leads all territories with 55 catalogued settlements, followed by Bukhara Core (42), Khiva (22), Turkmen Tribal Oases (20), Senior Zhuz (18), Eastern Bukhara (18), Middle Zhuz (9) and Junior Zhuz (8). Table \ref{tab:excluded-early-modern} details the 17 excluded candidate entries in the regional source ledger.

## Architectural Typology and Taphonomic Factors

Two material and archival factors condition early modern settlement analysis in this gazetteer [@Nurullayeva2025Timurid; @Anon2016Visions]. First, adobe mudbrick (*pakhsa*) construction, while thermally efficient in extreme continental climates, deteriorates rapidly when unmaintained [@Nurullayeva2025Timurid]. Following town abandonment or military sack (such as Saraishyk in 1580AD or Samarkand during the 1740AD crisis), unbaked brick walls quickly dissolve into amorphous earthen mounds (*tepe*), obscuring fine architectural stratigraphy unless excavated with modern stratigraphic methods [@Nurullayeva2025Timurid; @Rasulov2021Importance]. Only fired-brick monumental structures (minarets, portals and domed mausoleums) survive prolonged abandonment [@Nurullayeva2025Timurid].

Second, archival documentation across Central Asia exhibits sharp institutional divergences [@Anon2016Visions; @Wang2026Russian]. In Bukhara, legal contracts (*vasiqa*) and court registers (*daftars*) were preserved systematically in qadi archives, enabling precise tracing of urban property ownership and water distribution [@Anon2016Visions; @Gafurova2026Waqf]. In contrast, nomadic seasonal market locations and winter camps along the Syr Darya and Ural rivers left few formal municipal records, requiring retrospective calibration from nineteenth-century imperial Cossack frontier surveys and tribal genealogical registers [@Wang2026Russian; @Razdykov2019Appearance]. Consequently, settlement catalogues capture both permanent urban architecture and the dynamic trading nodes that mediated early modern Central Asian life [@StephanEmmrich2018Mobilities; @Chokobaeva2017Frontiers].
